summary:
A trans visitor to Montana stands under the United States national travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records. A visitor's documents may therefore mismatch presentation at the border or at checkpoints.

Screening carries an outing risk. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments responded: in April 2025 CNN reported that multiple countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.

Montana's own legal position is unusually favourable relative to its statute book. The state has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states for trans people, but Montana's courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined those laws under the state constitution. Adult restrictions that were enacted have consequently not taken full effect, and that court record improved Montana's standing in the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment. Montana was the only state to improve in the 2026 rankings.

The protections are judicial rather than statutory, so they depend on continued litigation. Nationally the youth-side picture remains unstable as federal policy shifts and litigation proceed. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19, in July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.
tangentialFactors:
Montana's trajectory runs against the national direction. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. Montana moved upward in the same assessment.

Document rules are tightening elsewhere. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. No equivalent Montana measure is sourced in this inventory.

Federal custody presents documented harm that does not depend on the state of residence. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse.

Official hostility at the national level is documented. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.
localsOnly:
Montana residents live under a set of enacted restrictions that have not been allowed to operate. The state has passed laws that would normally place it among the worst states, and the state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the Montana constitution, so adult restrictions that were passed have not taken full effect.

The state's improved standing in the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment rests on that court record rather than on the statutes themselves, and Montana was the only state to improve in the 2026 rankings. Any change in the composition or reasoning of Montana's courts would alter the position directly.

Nationally the youth-side picture is unstable because of federal policy shifts and continuing litigation, and residents seeking care for minors face measures including Executive Order 14187, the Department of Justice subpoenas to over 20 hospitals for records of patients under 19, the July 2025 shutdown of specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules that would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not identify which specific Montana statutes were blocked or enjoined, when each ruling issued, or which court issued it, so the subjects of the injunctions are unresolved here.

No sourced material covers changing the sex marker on a Montana birth certificate or driver's licence, and whether Montana issues an X marker on either document is unresolved in this inventory.

Nothing in the inventory establishes whether Montana operates state bathroom or facilities restrictions of its own, or how the federal single-sex facilities ban applies in Montana public buildings; the Movement Advancement Project figures cited are national totals and are not broken down for Montana.

No Montana-specific reporting on violence against trans people, police conduct, or hate-crime charges is available here, so state-level risk on those measures is not sourced.

The methodology and weighting behind the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, and the criteria separating the four states flagged "Do Not Travel," are not described in the sources.
